JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you very much, Prosecutor. Now I would like you to take the floor again to continue your speech and to tell us more about the relevant parts of the indictment. Can you hear the interpreter in the English booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I will now deliver my opening statement. In the Office of the Prosecutor, the charges in the indictment which we submit to the Trial Chamber today are referred to as "the shelling of Zagreb". For this shelling, Milan Martic, then the President of the self-proclaimed republic of Serbia Krajina, has been charged, in two separate counts, with violation of the laws and customs of war punishable under Article 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. One count deals with his order on May 2nd 1995 of an unlawful attack against the civilian population of Zagreb, and another count with his order on the following day, 3rd May, to the same effect, both causing numerous deaths and injuries to the population. Alternatively to each count, Milan Martic is charged under Article 7(3) of the Statute with failure, in his superior authority, to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the attacks and to punish the perpetrators of these attacks. In putting this shelling in an understandable context, I will start with giving an overview of the political and military circumstances in which the shelling took place. We had engaged an expert witness to do just that, but in the last minute, for personal reasons, the expert declined to testify. That leaves me to deliver the overview. Concerning factual matters such as confrontation lines, deployment of forces, placing of firing rockets, acquired maps and documents, we are going to bring as a witness one of the investors of the Prosecutor's Office, Mr Kevin Curtis, who at an early stage of the investigation was put on that task. It is, of course, impossible in the context of an opening statement in a Rule 61 hearing to give a full and detailed background to the fact that an armed conflict erupted between the Republic of Croatia and Krajina Serbs on the territory of Croatia in the beginning of May 1995. In more detail, that historical background is set out in a brief submitted to the Trial Chamber yesterday. Some outlining facts might serve the purpose to facilitate the understanding. By the late 1980s, ethnic tensions emerged in many parts of the former Yugoslavia, not least in Croatia, where Croat Serbs protest actions against alleged Croat repressions took place. The multi-party elections in the republics of Yugoslavia brought strong nationalist parties, which accelerated disintegration of the Federal Republic. As Macedonia and Slovenia had done, Croatia followed in the referendum and declared its independence in June 1991. The Serbian minority of Croatia, approximately half a million people, boycotted the referendum. They already had had one of their own, forming the Serbian autonomous region of Krajina, and declared on 1st October 1990 their autonomy and thus independence from Croatia. The Krajina Serbs mobilised to protect themselves, and in response Croatia did the same, and in October/November 1990 an armed conflict erupted between the parties in many parts of Croatia. After the declaration of independence of Croatia in June 1991, fighting between the Croatian armed forces and the army of Krajina Serbs intensified. The Krajina Serbs, since February 1991 the Serbian republic of Krajina, were extensively supported by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its army. Serbian paramilitary groupings with close links to that army also assisted the Krajina Serbs. The armed conflict continued for the duration of 1991 and resulted in the Serbs seizing approximately 25 per cent of the territory of Croatia. During this time, the Hague Peace Conference had failed to achieve peace, and the situation had deteriorated to such an extent that an arms embargo was imposed on Yugoslavia by the Security Council on 25th September 1991. At the beginning of October 1991, nevertheless, the siege of Dubrovnik commenced and attacks were launched on Vukovar by the Yugoslavian National Army. The armed conflict in Croatia ended in early 1992 with the adoption and implementation of the Vance plan. Under this agreement, a ceasefire was established which maintained the Serb-Croat territorial lines, but called for the peaceful reintegration of Serb-held territories back into Croatia and the return of all refugees. Furthermore, a United Nations multi-national peace-keeping force (UNPROFOR) was established and deployed into four United Nations Protection Areas, namely Sectors South, North, West and East, which covered almost all the Republic of Serbia and Krajina. Despite the Vance Plan, numerous violations of the January 1992 ceasefire occurred as hostilities between the Croatians and the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina sporadically erupted during 1992 and 1995. New negotiations were constantly arranged and various agreements were reached. The ceasefire agreement of 29th March 1994 was the most recent agreement before the attacks against Western Slavonia and the rocket attacks on Zagreb, now in question, in the beginning of May 1995. On 1st May 1995, the Croatian army, called HV, launched a massive attack from the west, east and north against the Serb-held territory in Western Slavonia. This area was one of the component parts of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It lies directly along the Zagreb-Belgrade highway, which is the principal east-west artery in Croatia. The part of the highway passing through Western Slavonia had remained closed to traffic from the end of the fighting in early 1992 until January 1995. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Excuse me, Prosecutor, during your speech would you use the video to show us the map? That would help both the Tribunal as well as the public. Will you be using the video to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We will do that. I will not say very much on the local surroundings, but in the first witness examination we will bring all the maps over the areas in question, but now I just mention where it is, and we will come back to that in examination of the witnesses, then use the facilities to do so. When I now mention the highway, I just give an outline where it goes through between these two cities. After negotiations between the Croats and the Serbs, the highway was reopened in late April 1995. However, several violent incidents occurred on the highway, which led to its closure again by the Serbs. The Croatian attack on Western Slavonia followed shortly after that decision. Within a few days after the attack, the forces of the Serbian Krajina were defeated and the Croats overran Sector West. Most of the Croatian Serb population of Western Slavonia fled the area for Sector East and the Serb held territories of Bosnia as a result of the attack. On the second and 3rd May 1995, while the fighting was still ongoing in Sector West, the city of Zagreb was shelled. The accused, Milan Martic, ordered these attacks, and he has publicly announced his responsibility for them. Who is, then, Milan Martic, and how did he become President of the Republic of Serbian Krajina with the power to do so? He was the chief of police in Knin in the Serbian populated part of Croatia, but was dismissed after the victory of the nationalist Croatian Democratic Union Party in the Parliamentary elections in April 1990, which led to the removal of Croatian Serbs from Office. He was instrumental in forming the Serbian National Council in the summer of 1990 and was a member of this Council from the outset. In January 1991, he was appointed secretary of the aforementioned Serbian autonomous region of Krajina, adopted in October 1990. He was in charge of the mobilisation of the Krajina Serbs to protect themselves. The Krajina Serbs adopted, in February 1991, their own constitution for the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which combined the Serb regions of Krajina, Slavonia, Baranja, West Srijem and West Slavonia. Martic was appointed Minister of Defence for that never recognised Republic. On 23rd January 1994, he was elected President of the Republic and thereby also, in accordance with the Constitution, Commander in Chief of the armed forces in war and peace. The Republic of Serbian Krajina is considered to have resolved in August 1995, after all parts of it except eastern Slavonia and some neighbouring areas had been overrun by the Croatian army. Milan Martic's position and whereabouts today is unclear. Some information indicates that he now lives in Banja Luka. At the attacks on Zagreb, a weapon known as Orkan (that is, in English, Hurricane) M-87, produced in the former Yugoslavia, was used. The Orkan is a rocket, launched, mounted on a cross -- JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Excuse me, sorry to interrupt, Prosecutor. You say that Mr Martic is at Banja Luka. Where is this? I think this would be interesting to hear. Did you say he is in Banja Luka? Is that the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When I return to this rocket, Orkan, which means Hurricane, I take the Yugoslavian name Orkan when I go on with this, this is a rocket launched on a cross-country truck, thus easy to move and to hide, which can be loaded with twelve rockets fitted with warheads containing 288 bomblets, all of which in turn have 400 small steel balls, which are scattered, along with bomblet fragments, on a lethal radius of ten metres. The range of the rocket is a maximum 50 kilometres. The area of impact of one rocket on the ground is an ellipse of 150 by 200 metres. It is used for soft targets, that is troops on the ground and vehicles, not for buildings or military installations, in other words an antipersonnel weapon. I will not go into further details. For that purpose, the military use of the weapon and the effect of it on the target, we are bringing Artillery Major Ted Itani from Canada as an expert witness, when we, of course, would show these things and how it works, and show pictures of it and go into details of it. On the first day of the attack, that is 2nd May last year, a Tuesday, six Orkan rockets fitted with warheads as previously described were launched against Zagreb. These rockets impacted at about 10.30 in the morning, mainly in central areas of the city, all heavily trafficked locations within the central commercial district. It caused the death of 5 civilians and injured another 186. Buildings and trams were hit, windows broken and at least 100 cars damaged. On the following day, Wednesday the 3rd, another six rockets were launched and, again, the centre of the city was hit at lunchtime. This attack caused the death of two persons and injured another 50. And, again, buildings, trams and cars were damaged. For detailed accounts of the casualties and damage of the two rocket attacks, we will bring two Croatian police officers as witnesses. They have both experienced attacks and took part in the investigation of the impact of them. On the 1st, 2nd and 3rd of May, the Croatian cities of Karlovac and Sisak were also attacked upon the orders of Milan Martic, but other weaponry than the Orkan rocket was used at that time. There were civilian casualties, but it has not been established whether the attack was of military significance. The Prosecution is not in the position to label it an attack on the civilian population and, consequently, has not incorporated it in the indictment. However, the use of the Orkan rockets against Zagreb underlines that that type of weapon was selectively chosen to attack and terrorise the civilian population. I will now proceed by addressing some legal issues pertaining to the indictment. Milan Martic is charged with being responsible for unlawful attacks against the civilian population and individual civilians of Zagreb, contrary to Article 3 of the Statute of our Tribunal, which permits the Tribunal to prosecute persons committing violations of the laws and customs of war. In the decision of the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal on 2nd October 1995 on the Tadic jurisdictional motion, the Appeals Chamber addressed the scope of Article 3 at some length, particularly in paragraphs 94, 126, and 143 of the majority judgment. In brief, the Chamber indicated that Article 3 was a general or residual clause covering all violations of humanitarian law not falling within Articles 2, 4 or 5. It indicated that, where violations of humanitarian law were embodied in customary international law, some customary law rules applied exclusively to international conflicts, some to internal conflicts and some to all conflicts. Further, it indicated that, where violations of humanitarian law were referred to in treaties, it must be established that the treaties were binding on the parties at the time of the alleged offence. It is the submission of the Prosecution that the existence of an armed conflict involving the armed forces of Croatia and the armed forces of the self-proclaimed Republic of Serbian Krajina is indisputable. The only question which might be raised is: is the conflict internal or international? Whether, on the basis of the evidence we are going to present during this hearing, the Trial Chamber will conclude that the conflict is internal or international, the offences remain the same. If the conflict is international, Article 85 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Convention prohibits making the civilian population or individual civilians the object of attack in international armed conflicts, and Additional Protocol I was in force as a result of ratification by the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1979 and accession by Croatia on 11th May 1992. If the conflict is internal, Article 13 of Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Convention prohibits making the civilian population or individual civilians the object of attack in internal conflicts, and Additional Protocol II was in force as a result. Accession by Croatia, also, on 11th May 1992. Further, if it is not considered practicable to classify the conflict as international or internal, the Appeals Chamber has indicated, in paragraphs 110, 111 and 112 of the majority judgment of the Tadic jurisdictional motion, that the principles of the UN General Assembly Resolutions 2444 of 19th December 1968, and 2675 of 9th December 1970, are part of customary law and applicable to all conflicts regardless of classification. Both of these resolutions indicate that it is prohibited to launch attacks against the civilian population as such. It is the submission of the Prosecution that the charges alleged against the accused can be committed in both international and internal conflicts, although the underlying legal basis for the charges varies depending on the nature of the conflict. I will now, as the concluding part of my opening statement, turn to the doctrine of reprisals. I have just stated that it is the submission of the Prosecution that it is prohibited to launch attacks against the civilian populations as such. It is also the submission of the Prosecution that reprisals against civilian populations or civilians are prohibited under international law, whether in international or internal armed conflicts. In the alternative, it is submitted that, to the extent that such reprisals may not be prohibited, they constitute an exception to the general rule of humanitarian protection and, consequently, their lawfulness is conditioned on the satisfaction of certain very strict criteria. In 1970, the General Assembly of the United Nations unanimously adopted resolution 2675 on: "Basic principles for the protection of civilian populations in armed conflicts", provided expressly that, "civilian populations, or individual members thereof should not be the object of reprisals, forcible transfers, or other assaults on their integrity." Although resolutions of the General Assembly are not considered legally binding when they are concerned with principles of international law, a unanimous or majority vote constitutes an important expression of opinio juris. Thus, the Appeals Chamber of the Tribunal considers resolution 2675 as, I quote the decision on jurisdiction on the Tadic case, page 61, paragraph 112: "Declaratory of the principles of customary international law regarding the protection of civilian populations and property in armed conflict of any kind". With respect to the minimum humanitarian standards under customary law, the dichotomy between international and internal armed conflicts is increasingly untenable. I quote again from the same decision of the Appeals Chamber, page 54, paragraph 97: "A state-sovereignty-oriented approach has been gradually supplanted by a human-being-oriented approach... It follows that, in the area of armed conflict, the distinction between interstate wars and civil wars is losing its value as far as human beings are concerned. Why protect civilians from belligerent violence, or ban rape, torture or the wanton destruction of hospitals, churches, museums, or private property, as well as proscribe weapons causing unnecessary suffering when two sovereign States are engaged in war, and yet refrain from enacting the same bans or providing the same protection when armed violence has erupted 'only' within the territory of a sovereign State? If international law, while of course duly safeguarding the legitimate interests of States, must gradually turn to the protection of human beings, it is only natural that the aforementioned dichotomy should gradually lose its weight." The 1977 Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions of 1949 provides in categorical terms that in an international armed conflict, "Attacks against the civilian population or civilians by way of reprisals are prohibited". Article 52, paragraph 1, of the same Protocol, provides that, "Civilian objects shall not be the object of attack or of reprisals." The former Yugoslavia and the Republic of Croatia ratified Protocol I in 1979 and 1992 respectively. Consequently, Protocol I was applicable for the entire duration of the armed conflict throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, including Croatia, and may thus be considered as part of the "laws or customs of war" within the meaning of Article 3 of our Statute. The 1977 Protocol II, also to the Geneva Conventions, defines the "fundamental guarantees" in Article 4, paragraph 1, that: "Persons who do take a direct part or who have ceased to take part in hostilities... shall in all circumstances be treated humanely", and in Article 13, paragraph 1, it goes on: "The civilian population, and individual civilians shall enjoy the general protection against the dangers arising from military operations", and then it goes on again: "The civilian population as such, as well as individual civilians, shall not be the object of attack. Acts or threats of violence, where the primary purpose of it is to spread terror among the civilian populations, are prohibited." It is significant that the International Committee of the Red Cross as the "guardian" of international humanitarian law has adopted the position that the prohibitions on inhumane treatment under Article 4 of Protocol II, "are explicit and do not allow for any exception", because, "They are absolute obligations" from which "no derogation is allowed", and consequently, "there is, in fact, no room left at all for carrying out 'reprisals' against protected persons". All this is quoted from the ICRC Commentary to Protocols, for these Protocols of the Geneva Convention. The ICRC observes that the absence of an express reference to "reprisals" in Protocol II is because of "reasons of legal and political nature" and that in the absence of such provisions, reprisals against civilians are "implicitly prohibited". I stressed that the lawfulness of reprisals was subject to strict criteria. A concise statement of these criteria or general rules, including those incorporated in most national law of war manuals, is contained in Chapter G of the ICRC Handbook on the Law of War for Armed Forces, generally called the "ICRC Handbook", which is extensively quoted in the brief on applicable law which we have submitted to the Trial Chamber. It is the submission of the Prosecution that, to the extent that reprisals against civilians may not be prohibited in internal armed conflicts, reprisals constitute a narrow exception to the general rule that civilians should be protected against inhumane acts and attacks under all circumstances. Consequently, the lawfulness of reprisals against civilians is conditioned on the strict satisfaction of certain criteria, such that a breach of any of the conditions would render the action unlawful. It is the submission of the Prosecution that reprisals against civilians constitute such a significant deviation from the elementary norms of international humanitarian law, that if serious or deliberate attacks on civilians are established beyond a reasonable doubt, there is a presumption that such action was unlawful in the absence of proof to the contrary. This issue is, in more detail, argued in a brief on applicable law submitted to the Trial Chamber yesterday. I conclude my opening statement by saying: the shelling of Zagreb was not a reprisal. It was a terror retaliation and it was unlawful. Thank you, your Honour. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Prosecutor, thank you. I have a question to put to you as regards reprisal. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): We all agree that the ICIC defined "reprisals" as a response to the breach of the law of war as a reply to a breach of that law by the enemy. Through your statements now and submissions, could you give us a better definition why there was an additional breach of the Republic of Croatia, because that did not seem so clear to me. The notion of reprisal is closely linked to the fact that those who are suspected or accused, in this case Mr Martic, can say that he was acting because he was a victim himself. In your submissions, Prosecutor, can you show that this breach as regards the law of war was not in any way very important and could not justify in one way or another the rocket that was launched. And the second question is whether you consider, when we talk about the prohibition of this arm by international legislation, there are lists of arms and weapons that are prohibited and there are some that are not, which does not mean that you have to use them, but the problem in international law is specific on this point. There are weapons which are not banned and others that are. So these are the two questions which I would like to put to you and my colleagues will no doubt put other questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I start with the last one. If I understood it rightly, we are maintaining that this weapon used against the civilians, the attack against the civilians was not a prohibited weapon, but it was prohibited to use it in the way it was used against the civilian population. I have not stated, we are not submitting to you that this is a weapon prohibited in any convention, just that you cannot use it on the civilian population in the way it was used. The other question is a very big question, of course, and I think we had tried to make it clear that a reprisal, in the way that reprisal is used in the international law, cannot be used in this way. I have been referring to the criteria and the criteria for using it are enumerated by the ICRC in their Handbook. We have it in the text we submitted to you. Our submission is that Martic, or the forces he represented, did not take any of these measures that should be used to make it legal to use this kind of force and to make it a reprisal. I repeat what I said, that this is, in my opinion, the submission of the Prosecutor, this is not a reprisal. I turn to the question, and I think it is proper to discuss this question, but, in the submission of the Prosecutor, we are not dealing with a reprisal. We are dealing with a retaliation and an unlawful one, and there were no foundations, not in the international law, to use these measures against the civilian population in the way that it happened. In more detail, your Honour, you will find arguments for this standpoint in the legal brief that we submitted to you. Thank you. utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, preliminarily, you asked about the issues that are going to be covered factually during the course of this proceeding. It is the position of the Prosecution that the attack, the Orkan missile rocket attack on the city of Zagreb on May 2nd and May 3rd was an unlawful attack on the civilian population. It is unlawful for several reasons. The first reason is, putting aside the reprisal issue, the first reason is that it was, in fact, an attack in an area where there are no legitimate military targets. The evidence that you are about to hear, your Honours, will detail photographs, video and testimony that will describe the city of Zagreb and the surrounding areas and, quite clearly, at the end of those facts and at the end of those photographs and at the end of that testimony, the court will unquestionabl see that there were no legitimate military targets in those areas. Assuming for the sake of argument that someone could argue that a building in downtown Zagreb, at noon, in the middle of the day, where civilians are walking around, assuming that is a legitimate military target, quite clearly the wrong weapons system was used to attack that building. If one was going to destroy a military target, such as a communications centre, or such, as some type of facility on an army base, the type of weaponry that would be used would not have been an Orkan rocket manned with a clustered bomb system, a system that was clearly designed, in this particular instance, your Honour, to kill civilians in downtown Zagreb and to otherwise put a reign of terror through that city to scare them into submission. That quite clearly will be the facts that will be presented throughout witnesses, your Honour. That, in short, the violations of the laws and customs of war on both the 2nd and 3rd. Your Honour, with the court's permission we will bring our first witness in. It is Detective Sergeant Kevin Curtis. KEVIN CURTIS, sworn

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you, Mr Curtis. Would you like to start your statement, unless the Prosecutor would like to start off with some questions straightaway. Mr Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. With the court's permission, I will begin with questions of Detective Sergeant Curtis. Good morning, Detective Sergeant Curtis.

utterances.text: And during your service in the British police force, where did you serve and what did you do on a daily basis?

utterances.text: I served in the area of Warwickshire, and on a daily basis, for the last twelve years, I have been investigating crimes of a serious nature, which include murder, rape, organised crime.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant, when did you come and work for the Prosecutor's Office for the International Law Crimes Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was seconded by the British Government as of 1st May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Since that time, give the court an idea of the general areas that you have been working on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have worked exclusively on incidents that have occurred during the course of the war, in the area of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Detective Sergeant, during your service, did you work on the missile attack on the city of Zagreb that took place on May 2nd and 3rd of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was my first assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: During working on that as an investigator, did you come to learn the situation militarily within the country of Croatia prior to the attack on May 2nd 1995 and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Will the use of some maps that you have before you assist you during the course of your explanation of the military situation in Croatia, prior and after the attack on May 2nd, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: With the court's permission, we would like to put the three maps into evidence, Prosecutor's Exhibit 1, Prosecutor's Exhibit 2 and Prosecutor's Exhibit 3. We would also ask if Sergeant Curtis could use the ELMO system to put these maps on the screen during the course of his explanation. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Prosecutor, first, while Sergeant Curtis gets the maps ready, I have an impression that the French interpreters are speaking extremely quickly. I would like to thank them and congratulate them for that. So could I kindly ask you to speak very, very slightly more slowly. The interpreters in the French booth are not machines, they are not robots, and it is my impression that they are speaking incredibly quickly. Would you mind speaking slightly more slowly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do apologise, your Honour, it seems that in every court room, in every case throughout the world, I have the same complaint. With all due respect, I will slow down. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): You see, that just proves that this is an International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Detective Curtis, can we move to Exhibit 1 and then proceed through Exhibits 1, 2, 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As can be seen by Exhibit 1, the area of Croatia is the lighter shaded area, which is clearly defined. We move on to exhibit number 2, which shows again the boundaries of Croatia, but we can see from here that this area stretching from the area of Knin right the way round to Western Slavonia is shaded in pink. That is the area that was occupied by the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: By the RSK, you mean the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Can I just say, there, not to be confused with the area inside of Bosnia, because that was not covered by the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: That was the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to the missile attack in May 1995, had the Republic of Serb Krajina attempted to secede from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you explain approximately during their secession how much of Croatia had been taken over by the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As can be seen from the map in front of you, approximately 25 per cent of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: This map depicts the situation prior to the missile attack, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map is dated late January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning your attention, Mr Curtis, to Exhibit 3, the situation after May 1995, can you show us what happened on the map and describe what transpired in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, again, as you can see, there is a pink shaded area reaching from the area of Knin right the way round, but on this occasion there is no occupation of the RSK within Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What happened between these two maps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 1st May 1995, there was an offensive by the Croatians against the area of Western Slavonia that was occupied by the RSK, which resulted in the RSK being pushed out of that area and Croatia taking over control once again.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: At this time, May 2nd 1995, do you know who the President of the RSK was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: He is the defendant in this particular indictment, is he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning your attention, if you would, to Prosecutor's Exhibit 4, which is the Constitution of the RSK, does that Constitution at any point set forth what the powers of the President are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Where is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It sets forth in great depth in Article 78, in particular interrelation to this case, page 14, Article 78, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What does that Constitution say concerning the powers of the President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It states that the President of the Republic of Serb Krajina commands the armed forces in peace and during the state of war, commands national resistance during a state of war, issues orders for general and partial mobilisation, organises defence preparations in compliance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, based on that, that Milan Martic was, in fact, the Commander in Chief of the armed forces as well as the President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I will offer into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 4, the Republika Srpska Constitution, as well as the translation in French of the pertinent paragraphs. Prior to the attack, on May 2nd 1995, had anybody in the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina indicated what the position of the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina would be, if the army was attacked in any way, shape or form by Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a statement by General Milan Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention -- is that statement set forth in a March 24th, 1995 article in a newspaper, a Serbian newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to that newspaper article, and the French translation set forth in Prosecutor's Exhibit 5. Do you have that before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, prior to reading that, we will offer Prosecutor's Exhibit 5 into evidence. Who is the General of the army who is talking in that article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milan Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Who is Milan Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is the General of the RSK army, or he was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: In the course of that article, does General Celeketic on March 4th, 1995, indicate what actions the Krajina Serbs would take in response to any war-like acts by the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you go to that point of the article and read that into record, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is page 4, the last question on the page .

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you read that question, Sergeant Curtis, and the answer given by General Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the question is: "The notorious Ustasha, Sime Dodan, recently commenting on the alleged threats from the Krajina Serbs, as he put it, to launch rockets on Croatian towns if new Ustasha aggression is launched, announced: 'They should be aware that we know where these rockets are and where Belgrade is...' General, how would you, as the leader of the Serbian Army of Krajina reply to this?" General Celeketic replied: "You are now provoking me a little, but I will tell you what I think about it. I believe I am quite a reasonable man, and I talk only with reasonable people, even if they are on the opposite, enemy side. I believe that that is not the case here, but let us not go into this sort of discussion. In case of Ustasha aggression, we will certainly not miss the opportunity to hit them where it hurts the most. We know their weak spots and where it hurts the most. Weak points are city squares and we know who goes there -- civilians. I have already said this and was criticised a little. Well now, they may ask, which squares and in which cities? I shall reply that that is a military secret. We shall make a decision about it, and I think we will be precise. It is hard to say these words, because there are, as I said, civilians in the squares, innocent people. However, if we are at war (and we are waging a filthy war for which they are first and foremost to blame) then there will be no mercy. Not only will we be merciless, but as a commander I will decide where we will direct our attacks, when and where it hurts the most. As for what the gentleman says about Belgrade, he must know what he means by it. I would not comment on it."

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Does that same article, at any point, Sergeant Curtis, indicate by General Celeketic who was his Commander in Chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the same page, page 5, the last question states: "Finally, General, tell us about your co-operation with the supreme military commander of the Republic of Srpska Krajina Armed Forces, President Milan Martic." General Celeketic replied: "The co-operation with my Supreme Commander General, Milan Martic, is excellent. One could only wish for such a superior".

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: At the time of the attack on Zagreb on May 2nd and 3rd, who was the military commander for the Army of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Milan Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: As an investigator, was that article of any significance to you while you were investigating that crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because threats had been made that if there was any Croatian offensive against the RSK, then the cities would be bombed and, in fact, that is what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to exactly what happened. On May 2nd and 3rd of 1995, what happened in the city of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On May 2nd and 3rd, on each day, six Orkan rockets were fired on the city of Zagreb, which resulted in a number of civilians dying, and a large number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: At this juncture, I would ask if I could give you a map and explain to the court in some detail exactly where these bomblets fell. I am showing you for the record Prosecutor's Exhibit 6. Using Prosecutor's Exhibit 6, Sergeant Curtis, are you aware of the various locations where the Orkan rocket bomblets fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you use a pointer and explain to the court exactly what transpired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2nd May, as I stated, six rockets landed in the area of the city of Zagreb. They were number 1, here, number 2, number 3, which is clearly right in the city centre, and three further ones here in the area of Pleso, the airport. On the second day, two more, numbers 4 and 5 here, landed on the city centre, and also three in this area, which is just on the outskirts of the city centre, and a further one which is down the bottom here.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I will offer into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 6. You may have a seat, Sergeant Curtis, based on your investigation, are you aware of the damage that took place in those various locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Many vehicles were damaged, either as a result of direct hits or spray from the bomblet that comes from the Orkan missile, and many buildings were scarred and damaged and windows broken also, either by direct hits or spray from the Orkan bomblet.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: How about casualties, deaths?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over the two days, seven civilians died as a result and there were well over 100 heavily wounded and well over 100 which were lightly wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Detective Curtis, during the course of your investigation of the Zagreb rocket attack, did you visit virtually all of these locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I visited most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see any military installations in any of these locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: When you examined these various locations, what type of individuals were walking around those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just the normal civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you what has been marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 7. I will hand it to the clerk. (Handed). Do you know what Prosecutor's Exhibit 7 is, Detective Sergeant Curtis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the actual bomblets that landed within the city centre of Zagreb during the attack we are talking about, and it failed to explode and has been deactivated.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on your investigations, do you have some preliminary idea of how the Orkan rocket system worked with these cluster bombs in the warhead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The rocket contains approximately 288 of these bomblets, and when it gets to a certain height, the mechanism within the rocket allows these bomblets to fall from the main rocket body. These have a charge within them and the operation is that when they fall down the ribbon here turns and it turns a screw which effectively forms the firing pin, so that when it hits the ground the firing pin goes down and this bomblet, which has over 400 tiny ball bearings, will explode 360 degrees and these tiny balls, together with scrap metal from the bomblets, will go off at great speed in all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that, in fact, one of the bomblets that failed to go off during that attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we will offer Prosecutor's Exhibit 7 into evidence. Sergeant Curtis, during the course of your investigation, did you obtain a video taken by law enforcement authorities in the city of Zagreb showing the various scenes on the 2nd and 3rd of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I received it from the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: With the court's permission, and your Honours', at this time we would like to play what has been marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 8, which is video footage, your Honours, of various scenes in Zagreb and the surrounding areas of the damage and some of the carnage, as well as people killed and murdered, that were killed on these two days. With the court's permission at this time, we would ask if the gentleman in the video room could play Prosecutor's Exhibit 8. (Video played). By way of explanation, your Honours, we are looking at various locations in downtown Zagreb where the bomblets exploded and damaged property. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): I have a question I would like to put to you, Mr Prosecutor, while we look at the video. The buildings which we see, are they all civilian buildings, or are there also buildings which could be regarded as military in character? Can you ask the witness the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant Curtis, the question that was asked by Judge Jorda is, as we are looking at these buildings, are any of these buildings military buildings or buildings that could be construed as military buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of the buildings are military buildings. There is a police station amongst them, but as every city has --

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge of how the Orkan works, if they were attempting to destroy the police headquarters, would they have used this type of warhead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is totally the wrong sort of warhead to use, as the Orkan missile is an anti-personnel missile.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: During your examination of these various areas, other than windows being destroyed and outside walls, did any of these bomblets knock down any buildings at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and they are not capable of doing so. As you can see here now, there is fire damage to vehicles, which is obviously a secondary thing to the actual -- what the rocket caused. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Prosecutor, I would like you to ask the witness another question. As a specialist in this area, could he perhaps tell us whether the Orkan rocket was used in other conflicts? Could he give us an example of when the Orkan would be used?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any situations, Detective Sergeant Curtis, where any Orkans were used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of them, but I am not an expert in this area, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can give the court an example of an area, certainly Major Itani can give the court some significant detail in this area. It is my understanding that it is designed to use against soft targets and open terrain, for instance, against advancing troops, advancing tanks, and advancing soft cover vehicles such as trucks, et cetera. I understand that it had been used during the Persian Gulf conflict. To what extent it was used, your Honour, I do not know. I will say, your Honour, that we could cover that subject in some detail with Major Itani when he testifies. Sergeant, this photograph of this dead civilian is right next to the tram, the public tram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. As is indicated in the top of the picture where it was chalked, it would appear that that is where the bomblet landed. We can also see indentations in the ground all around where the body is lying.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, in this location where this woman was murdered, were there any military targets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None whatsoever. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Prosecutor, I have a question on the bomblets. Are they round, or what sort of shape do they have?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The actual bomblets, your Honour, are exactly like that. That is just a disarmed bomblet. When they detonate when they hit the ground, they explode in an elliptical form, in 360 degrees. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): I am talking about the 420 steel pellets, the ball bearings. You have 282 bomblets, I suppose the small bomblet is like this, and if you could hand it over to us to have a closer look I would be interested. You talked about the 420 ball bearings. What I want to know is whether the 420 ball bearings are round, or what sort of shape they are, and, at the same time, if you could bring it to us so we could inspect it more closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you can see, your Honour, they are round. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): I have the answer I wanted, thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant, that is yet another dead civilian under that blanket, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. He was in the car at the time of the impact of the missile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: May I ask you something: is this tape the film after one attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Only one, your Honour. This is taking place on 2nd May 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Immediately after?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour . This, your Honour, was that other civilian that was just under the blanket. For the court's clarification, the video that proceeds -- we are about to look at another civilian that was killed, and the video that proceeds on to 3rd May 1995 again depicts numerous damage. The explosion that damaged an old aged home, and part of the explosion that damaged a children's hospital, part of the explosion that damaged the National Academy where dancers from various countries throughout the world were performing, and various other locations in downtown Zagreb. At this time, your Honour, I just would offer the entire video into evidence, and the Prosecutor sees no need at this juncture to play the rest of the twenty minutes after this particular third citizen is shown unless the court wants to see the rest of the video. In addition to the videos, we do have photographs for the court to examine, which also depict these scenes in various forms. So the Prosecution will be guided by the desires of the court to cut this short and proceed with the questioning and conclude the questioning, or to let it run approximately fifteen more minutes. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): We will consider that right now, if you do not mind. Mr Prosecutor, the court would like to know the impact it has on the civilians, on the victims, the innocent victims. Furthermore, we are aware of the nature of this video. What we ask you is, is it possible to see the actual photos of the victims because this will make us aware of the full impact? We have already seen the effect of two victims, and although it is very difficult, we would like to see the photos of the victims as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are no more victims on here. We have some photographs of some victims, and during the lunch hour we can get photographs of some victims at various locations. Some of those victims naturally, your Honour, were not photographed at the time, simply because they were rushed to the hospital, but we do have some photographs of some victims in our file that we can provide after lunch. With regard to the effect on the individual citizens, the witness that will come on next, Mr Tuksa, was the police officer who was there at the time who will be able to give testimony concerning the state of affairs in Zagreb and how the civilians were reacting during this entire attack on both days. Your Honour, would you prefer to stop the video at this point and conclude the questioning? JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Please you can resume your questions, and we would like to have the photos which you have mentioned. You can resume the questioning. Would you like to put the questions so that we are consistent? How much time do you need, so that we have a rough idea of when we should adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do believe that Sergeant Curtis will finish in five minutes with several follow-up questions introducing some things in evidence. It will be very brief. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Fine. We will proceed accordingly. We will do the rest of the testimony of Mr Curtis. Put your questions. Then we will adjourn until after lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant Curtis, after this attack took place, did the President of the Krajina Serbs, Milan Martic, say anything about these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he, in fact, said a number of things. He admitted to the fact --

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: I am sorry, say that again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He admitted to the fact that he was responsible for the rockets that were launched on Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you obtain a tape of his public statements to television crews after this attack took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a short video of that speech. It is Prosecutor's Exhibit 9. A transcript of that speech and its pertinent points are in Prosecution Exhibit 10 that is before the court. If we could play that very briefly. Before we play it, can we read the pertinent parts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit number 10, Mr Martic states: "Dear brothers and sisters, your holiness! I wish to address a couple of words to you to also tell you about the situation that has befallen us and what we plan to do in order to extricate ourselves from it all. First of all, I wish to tell you that I truly sympathise with all the suffering you have been through. I would have preferred the situation to be good, and that I were here to attend a wedding in Western Slavonia instead of coming here at the worst time for you to explain to you now how and in what manner we are to pull out and we are to find some way out of all this, so that you do not roam and we also keep our country. We had a meeting here with the civilian authorities and military leadership and with our archpriests. What Croatia has done to us is undoubtedly a crime, aided by the foreign powers of America and Germany. This was not a question of treason, but solely that our enemy was stronger at that moment and succeeded in taking control of the highway and also of this part you know about. But I say that one battle does not mean the war is lost. Because of what Tudman did to you, as a counter measure we bombarded all their cities: Sisak several times, Karlovac and Zagreb, yesterday and today. It was done for you, but let me inform you that the attack by Tudman's forces was not directed only against Western Slavonia. He attacked Lika and he attacked Dalmatia. Lika succeeded in defending itself. In Dalmatia, from the Dinara Mountain their forces were removed. An ultimatum was issued today to say that, if they continued attacking our besieged forces, we shall continue pounding Zagreb, and pound and further destroy their cities. After that, he begged that we stop attacking Zagreb and said that they would release our forces under siege... that is what interests you the most."

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we will play the tape which shows the defendant, Milan Martic, giving a speech. That is Prosecution exhibit number 9. (Video played). Sergeant, in addition to the television footage that we just saw that took place on 3st May 1995, did Martic make other admissions concerning the ordering of the attack on Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, in a radio interview accorded him on 5th May 1995 and also an interview which was published in the International Herald Tribune on 16th May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe you have a transcript of the radio interview as Prosecutor's Exhibit 11, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you read the pertinent parts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an interview given by Milan Martic to the so-called Serb radio, studio Petrova Gora broadcast on 5th May 1995 as part of the central news programme. He said: "I have nothing to hide. That order was given by me, personally, as a retaliation to Franjo Tudman and his staff for the order he had given to commit aggression against Western Slavonia and to commit a crime against the civilian population of Western Slavonia. What followed was our... my order to shell Zagreb and that was the decisive factor in stopping that aggression. The aggression has been stopped for the time being, and we are currently negotiating with UNPROFOR. As you know, an agreement has also been signed to allow our civilians and also our soldiers, but with their weapons, to get out of that territory and cross over to the Republika Sprpska."

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You, likewise, give a slightly different explanation to the International Herald Tribune in an interview published on May 16th 1995, and set forth in Prosecutor's exhibit number 12, which is also in translation before the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you read the pertinent parts to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interview was by John Pomfret of Washington Post Service, and in the relevant part, Mr Pomfret says: "In the interview, Mr Martic, 41, a former traffic policeman, said he felt justified in ordering the rocketing because he was aiming at military installations. 'I am very sorry if civilian targets were hit because our aim was to hit military targets', he said. 'But this was only a warning', Mr Martic insisted. 'If something happens in the future, we will not only hit military targets with our rockets, but launch inventory attacks at towns that were Serbian before -- like Karlovac and Osijek, two important Croatian cities'. In addition, he stressed that the Orkan attack was a mild response to the invasion."

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Does he explain anywhere what these military targets were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he does not.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: When you read these and came in contact with these particular articles, were they of some significance to you as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because, obviously, earlier in March, General Celeketic had threatened to bomb the cities if there was an offensive by the Croatians, and they did, and admissions have been made since that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Has Martic made a recent statement, as late as 24th February 1996, concerning his participation in this activity? I direct your attention to Prosecutor's exhibit 12A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he has.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you read the pertinent parts to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was in Banja Luka to Associated Press that he made this statement on 24th February this year. I refer you, your Honours, to paragraph 2, where it starts: "In an interview with Associated Press Television in the Bosnian Serb stronghold of Banja Luka on Friday, Martic admitted that he had ordered the bombing of the Croatian capital, Zagreb, on May 2nd and 3rd 1995, when at least six civilians were killed and some 160 wounded. 'I really did order the bombing of Zagreb and I will never deny it', Martic says, 'but I did that to save the convoys of refugees, women and children and the feeble, who the Croatian President Franjo Tudman ordered to be bombed by artillery and aviation. It is known that there were massive casualties. Are the lives of those people worthless compared to Zagreb and the people living there?' Martic asked". Then, your Honours, if we can go down to paragraph 9, which starts: "Martic claimed." "Martic claimed that the charges against him, Karadzic, Mladic, were politically motivated. 'I am one of the people who headed a state, just as Karadzic', Martic said. 'Through us, the entire Serb people is put on trial. I am judged by those responsible for the war in former Yugoslavia. To shed their own responsibility and guilt they have to put the blame on those who lost this war' he alleged. 'That is extreme cynicism'." Again, your Honours, if we can go down to paragraph 14, which begins: "Every attempt", near the bottom of the page: "'Every attempt to arrest me I will regard as a terrorist act, and I will respond adequately. There is no dilemma', Martic said. 'Under normal circumstances, I would have volunteered to go to The Hague to go on trial, but there is no honesty and justice there', he added".

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Detective Curtis, in all the time that you have been on this case and all the hours that you have spent examining various locations in and around Zagreb, have you come across anything resembling a military facility in all the places that were attacked and in all the locations where civilians were killed and injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing at all. It was just normal civilians walking about, going about their daily business.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Martic and the army of the RSK do on May 2nd and 3rd 1995 what Celeketic promised they would do on March 25th of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, subject to taking these photographs -- the witness need not get up from the court -- you are familiar from the cart to your left, Sergeant, Exhibits 13 through 33, which are various photo albums and maps? Are you familiar with those sergeant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Where did you obtain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the police in Zagreb and the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will examine those photographs and some of those maps at some length with our next witness, but at this time I have no further questions of Sergeant Curtis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Sergeant Curtis, you mentioned that as a result of the attack seven civilians were killed, 100 wounded heavily and 100 wounded lightly. Considering the nature of the bombs which you have explained and the number of the bombs and the vital sites, sections of the town, to which they were directed, would not the resulting damage have been normally much greater and much graver on the physical and moral level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I would consider that it was very fortunate that not many more people got injured or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Was this not one of the peak hours in the life of the city, or was it a dead hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, 10.25 on 2nd May is when the rockets landed in Zagreb, which is a peak time for people walking about, talking, as they do in their normal city life. On 3rd May, it was at 12.10, which was lunchtime, which would normally mean that there were many people about within the city centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may answer that with some additional information that we will get from Mr Petric, who is a pyrotechnician, he will testify that approximately 3,000 of those bomblets were dropped on the city, but there was a high failure right, luckily, on many of those bomblets. They have retrieved approximately 1,200 of them, either through their failure to go off or through his team's spreading out all over the city of Zagreb and defusing them prior to them going off. The way the bomblet works, your Honour, is if it lands on its side, if someone walks very closely and possibly shakes it, that could detonate it in and of itself. So because of the pyrotechnicians that went to the scene, they were able to defuse many of these before they exploded. We will also see some photographs, your Honour, that one of those pyrotechnicians lost his life and another lost his limb while they were trying to defuse these weapons. That is part of it. On the second day, on the 3rd, you will get this testimony from Mr Tuksa, the city of Zagreb was in a virtual panic after the attack that took place on the 2nd, and because of the panic, everybody stayed indoors and were not normally walking the streets. So while this explosion, or this attack on the 3rd took place at 12.10, because it took place on the second day, there was a decrease in pedestrian traffic in the normal parks and areas that were and around the city of Zagreb. So that luckily gave another reason why the fatalities on the second day were fewer than the first, and even the injuries on the second day were fewer than the first. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Prosecutor, a question to you and then another question to Sergeant Curtis. I wanted to be quite clear in our understanding, between the attack on the 2nd and 3rd May, am I correct there were 12 rockets, and 3,000 bombs? I want to be precise on the figures, how many rockets and how many bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On each day, your Honour, six rockets were fired. Within each rocket there are approximately 288 bomblets. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): A point of information, Sergeant Curtis, can you show with the pointer where we have the children's hospital and the old age home which you made allusion to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, your Honour. The children's hospital and the elderly person's residency are both very close together in the area around here, which occurred on 3rd May. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): You have the floor, Mr Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of Sergeant Curtis at this time. I ask that we break for lunch pursuant to your Honour's instructions and we will bring our next witness in, because he is the witness that needs the changes to be made in the court room in any event. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Fine. The meeting is adjourned, and we will start again at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Prosecutor, I see we have made the necessary arrangements, bearing in mind your request as regards the new witness. In order to allow the witness to enter, we would ask you to lower the curtains, perhaps, so that the witness can enter, take the oath and then once he is firmly installed we can lift the curtains up again. Please allow the witness to enter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a preliminary matter before that takes place. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to the lunch break, your Honour, you asked us to go back to our files and to produce some photographs of individual civilians that were injured and on the way to the hospital as a result of the attacks on 2nd and 3rd May 1995. Sergeant Curtis is in the court room now and we have marked for admission for the purposes of this hearing Prosecution Exhibits 39 through 44, and we would like to show them to the court on the monitor. We can start, Sergeant Curtis, with number 39. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): I would like to ask you the following question: must they be seen by the public, because, after all, they form in that domain? Is there no problem? Then Sergeant Curtis can present the documents on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Beginning with Exhibit 39. It is an elderly gentleman, your Honour, wounded obviously in the head, and bleeding down through the face. Can we turn to Exhibit 40, Sergeant Curtis? Another gentleman, who has blood wounds to the head. You can see the blood coming down the left side of his face and into the gentleman's ear as he is being taken into an ambulance and taken to the hospital. Prosecution Exhibit 41, Sergeant Curtis. This is an individual who, at this point, it is unknown whether or not he was one of the individuals that died on his way to the hospital, obviously seriously wounded, and the court can see the blood on his left hand at the bottom of the photograph. Exhibit 42 is that same individual with the blanket over him on the left as well as another gentleman with a bloodstained white shirt also being put in same ambulance and taken to the hospital. This is Exhibit 43, with an injured child being taken. It is unknown, your Honour, whether or not that is a relative, a good Samaritan, if you will. It is just unknown. The last one is of an elderly woman. If you examine the lower part of her dress you can see that there is blood dripping down both on her face and down on the left side of her dress on the right side of the photograph. All clearly civilians, your Honour, and injured in the attack on 2nd and 3rd May 1995. I believe, for the purposes of the record, those are Exhibits 39 through 44 inclusive. This time, with the court's permission, we would bring in Mr Franjo Tuksa. Your Honour, while we are waiting I would also ask the court's permission to allow Sergeant Curtis to remain in the court room so we more efficiently operate the ELMO system and move through some of the photographs with all due speed. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Could you remind me of his name, please? His name is Franjo -- could you tell me the name, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Franjo, F-r-a-n-j-o, Tuksa T-u-s-k-a, with -- I am not sure what the accent is called over the S. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Tuksa, please put your headsets on. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TUKSA
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you very well. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): You are now going to take the oath, which is being presented to you. FRANJO TUKSA, sworn

utterances.speaker: MR. TUKSA
utterances.text: JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you, please be seated, and could you please raise the curtains now? Mr Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr Tuksa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Original in Croatian) Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Tuksa what do you do for a living, what job do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked with the police department for the last twenty years. I have been employed at various posts from ordinary policeman up to the head, and I am head, in charge of war crimes and terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: As chief of war crimes and terrorism in the city of Zagreb, how many people do you have working for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten people there in my department. I am their chief.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Tuksa, let me direct your attention to May 2nd and 3rd of 1995. Were you working on those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was at work on both of those days, and I was in charge of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: And the whole situation -- by "the whole situation", what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything that was documented, all the reports went through my department and I sent them to the prosecutors in Croatia and to the Prosecutor in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us talk first about 2nd May 1995. Were you in your office at approximately 10.25 in the morning of 2nd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. I do remember. I will remember that day all my life. I was there about 10.25. It was Tuesday, a lovely sunny day.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard several explosions in Zagreb, and we heard them in my office too. One explosion landed about 100 metres from my office, and we can talk about it later.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you do after you heard the explosions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we heard the explosion, I and my colleagues ran to the Zrinjevac Park, where we saw several vehicles on fire. The firemen came, they had already arrived. They put out the fire, and in the Zrinjevac Park itself, there were bomblets all around the place. They were hanging from trees, bomblets.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What is this area of Zagreb like on a normal sunny day in May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the most urbanised part of Zagreb. The park itself is only about 100 metres from the main square in Zagreb, the Bana Square. The number of pedestrians is very high. For example, at the time of the explosion at Zagreb, the American Embassy was only 100 metres from there.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there any military installations or communication centres near that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I absolutely claim that in the centre of Zagreb there are no military installations of any kind whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately how many locations were hit with these bomblets from the Orkan rockets on May 2nd 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2nd May 1995, three rockets landed on the central part of Zagreb. While three others landed on the Pleso housing estate, a total of six rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know, based on your investigation, Mr Tuksa, how many people were killed and injured as a result of the rocket attack on 2nd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of the shelling on 2nd May, four civilians were killed on the spot. Later, in the hospital, about a month after, from injuries sustained on that occasion, an old pensioner died, so that on the first day the number of fatalities is five. The gentleman who died later, his name is Ivan Brodac.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: A rocket attack took place again on 3rd May, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The shelling was repeated again at 12.10 hours, on 3rd May, when I was also in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: As a result of that attack, are you aware of how many people were killed and how many people were injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the second day of shelling, on 3rd May, one policeman, a pyrotechnician, was killed on the spot, as he was defusing the bomblets near the children's hospital in the Klaiceva Street, and one student died later from wounds about a month after he sustained the wounds, a month after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So Mr Tuksa, as a result of the attack on 2nd and 3rd May, what was the total amount killed and total amount injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On both days, seven civilians were killed, seven civilians from Zagreb were killed. 124 were severely injured. 87 civilians had light wounds, light injuries. According to our reports, a total of 218 civilians, including the fatalities.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You distinguished between lightly injured and seriously injured. What is your distinction between seriously injured and lightly injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can certainly explain. Light injuries, the normal physiological functions are still okay. There are no permanent consequences. They are mostly scars and a light injury will never become a serious one, but in the case of serious injuries, one remains disabled and the functions, physiological functions have been damaged permanently. We have a case of two civilians who died from injuries sustained at the bombing, a severe injury very frequently ends in fatality.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So based on your investigation, Mr Tuksa, approximately 125 civilians have permanent damage as a result of that rocket attack, in addition to seven fatalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Yes, that is what I claim.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Tuksa, let me take you back to the city of Zagreb on May 2nd and May 3rd of 1995. What was the mood of the civilians on the street after these rockets hit the city of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the shelling of Zagreb, unfortunately I must admit that people were panic stricken. They were restless. There was a feeling that any minute you would be hit by something and you would be killed, and you have no idea why you are being killed. I am speaking on my own behalf, but I am fond of jogging, and those days, as I jogged, I looked to the sky wondering if something was going my way. I suppose that other citizens felt pretty much the same. People banned their children from going out, because they were panicked by fear of being shelled again. Indeed, I would not like to see any city experience what Zagreb has experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Tuksa, was anybody injured some months after the event of May 2nd and 3rd as a result of the bomblets that were fired on the city of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Almost three months after the event, after the incident, on 27th July 1995, at about 2000 at the Zitnjak part of Zagreb in the immediate vicinity of the location where, on 3rd May, a bomb exploded, the explosion which happened by accident. The explosion of a bomblet caused severe bodily injuries to the children Alen Kicic, Alen Prokic, Anto Saraf and Damir Jambresic. These children found an unactivated bomblet which remained after the bombing of 3rd May and they played with it without knowing anything about it and the explosion occurred. The consequences are those that I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: This was over two months after the bombing of Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two and a half months, on 20th July, which shows the really cunning aspect of this weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Tuksa, let me ask you preliminarily to take a look at this map of the city of Zagreb. Do you recognise that area, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, I do recognise this part of Zagreb, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
