utterances.text: Using the map and the pins that are before you, can you place on the map, Mr Tuk{a, the locations in downtown Zagreb where the bombs landed on the 2nd, and then the locations in downtown Zagreb when they landed on the 3rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I will use the red highlighter for the 2nd May. This is the central part of Zagreb which was hit by three rockets, the first day and the second day by two rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to ask you once again, in any of those locations, in your twenty years as a police officer, has there ever been a military installation in those locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There have never been any military installations. A European city like Zagreb does not have military installations in the centre of the city and Zagreb is definitely a European city.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Tuksa, let me turn our attention to a series of photographs that you provided to the Office of the Prosecution, starting with Prosecution Exhibits 13 and 14, as well as a series of maps, which is Prosecution Exhibit 31. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look at, first, the binders of photographs. I believe those are the photographs that you provided to the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those are the locations where rockets landed. The rocket which landed on the first day, that is the site where there was the largest number of fatalities.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: How many fatalities were there in this area, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that area, there were, as we see from the picture, three civilians killed in the street, and during the investigation they were still in the street and one civilian was taken by the ambulance, so we can speak about four fatalities at the intersection of Sostariceva Street, Vlaska Street and Mrazoviceva Street. I would also like to point out that a lady by the name of Ana Mutevelic was killed at the very corner here. She was riding the tram, tram 12, in the first carriage of the tram, at the back part of the carriage, when a bomblet pierced the roof of the tram and killed a woman who was later carried out by the civilians onto the pavement of Vlaska Street. Her name is Ana Mutevelic.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Tuksa, if you could, could you turn to the binder that is in Prosecution Exhibit 13?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is, I can see on the monitor, the lady who is lying prostrated in Vlaska Street, Ana Mutevelic is her name.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: That is in there as F38 in your book, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, F38, yes, you are right, the person who rode in the tram several moments ago and died as an innocent civilian. She has a degree in law.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did she have anything to do with the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely nothing. A civilian, she is a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the photographs of your law enforcement officers working for you, and I am talking about F42, 43 and 44.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Do those photographs depict the type of injuries that an Orkan rocket inflicts, specifically 42, 43 and 44?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you put those quickly on the monitor? We are looking at this point at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are the injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to 43 and 44.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: There is another individual who was killed shortly thereafter, whose photographs are in F57 through 60. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the late Damir Dracic, who probably got out of his car, because that was his car in the vicinity, and he was hit by a bomblet. I am aware of the fact that he was waiting for his wife who had been shopping in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Do F62 and 63 also demonstrate the type of injuries that are sustained from these bomblets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they do. Doctors call this explosion wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could request 62 and 63, which are better copies to show on the monitor than mine, F62 and 63. F62 shows the head wound and 63 the wounds to the hand. If I might turn your attention, Mr Tuksa, to F140 in your book, F140. We see, do we not, the type of injuries from the Orkan rocket bomblet when it explodes, do we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the type of injury caused by the explosion of bomblets. These deceased were photographed in the emergency hospital in Draskoviceva Street, which is in the immediate vicinity of the place where they were killed, maybe 100 metres from the site.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: That is Prosecution Exhibit 13. Turning your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 14 in the other binder of photographs, do you have that up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to Prosecution Exhibits 15 through 20, as well as the plan, which is plan 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photo documentation which I have in my hand shows Matice Hrvatske Street, if that was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that, likewise, in the city of Zagreb, downtown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is about 100 metres from my office. It is the centre of the city, the very centre of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look through the rest of the photographs in sequence. I am talking about Prosecution Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are streets in the immediate vicinity of the site of shelling on 2nd May, Mrazoviceva Street, where vehicles were damaged, window panes of business facilities, windows of business facilities. There were no casualties, no fatalities, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: How about the next binder of photographs, Prosecution Exhibit 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This shows Petrinjska Street, where many civilians were killed or sustained serious or light wounds. Property was damaged, windows, glass in the windows. Thousands of individuals walk along this street. It is a very, very busy street in Zagreb, and I myself walk along that street many times because I go to a restaurant in this street during my lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look at the balance of those photographs. Are they all approximately in the same location, Mr Tuksa, and do they all depict various areas where the bomblets exploded in the city in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: They show various places where property damage took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: That is fine. We have completed with those.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything is identical, but you do not have the frequency of movements of civilians, because the photograph was taken afterwards, because at this time the civilians were mostly in shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to 21 and 22, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have 20. I only have 21.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: We will just move to 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This shows damage done to the vehicles in the immediate vicinity of Vlaska and Mrazoviceva Streets, where the major impact took place. This is Ribnjak Street, a very, very busy street in the city of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn your attention to the next bundle of photographs and Prosecution Exhibit 22. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, 22.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What do those photographs show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They show the site, the location of the third explosion on the first day, if I can call it that. This is the well-known -- the best known high school in Zagreb, the so-called Classical Gymnasium, which has been attended by many from Zagreb. It shows the location of the explosion and the place where the rocket landed, exactly on the playground of this school. Fortunately, there was nobody there, there were no children, so there were no serious consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us look at the photographs F5 through F8. Is that the school yard where the bomblet exploded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the school yard.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move through these photographs. What is that on the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are scars on the walls from explosions by bomblets, or ball bearings contained within the bomblets which spray out.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: How about the next two, F7 and F8?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also the school building, with the damage shown on its facade.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you explain, Mr Tuksa, how fortunate those children were not to have been killed in that school yard on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a school interval, recess, break, and there was a difference of five minutes between the break and the time of the lesson. This school yard is usually used -- there were supposed to be over 100 students, pupils, from that school which could have had very tragic consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: We are talking about Exhibits 23, 24, 25, 26 and 27. We might as well go through 28 and 29, as they are the last two on this point. Starting, Mr Tuksa, with Exhibit 23, do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it is not on the monitor, just on the photographs that you have in your hand. What are those photographs that are in Exhibit 23 that are right before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not have the exhibit numbered 23.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You do not have 23?

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: There should be 23 there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I have number 23.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us talk about Exhibit 23. What are those photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is still the shelling of the 2nd May, the suburb of Pleso, the vicinity of the Zagreb airport. There are many residential houses here. There are no residential buildings, just family houses. Twenty-three family houses were damaged in this area, according to what I remember. There were several slightly and severely wounded citizens, civilians, there were no fatalities, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, that location is not a military target, any military installations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The suburb of Pleso has no military installations, it is a very quiet neighbourhood, there are no military installations here. In the vicinity there is the airport, which is also called Pleso, Zagreb airport, Pleso.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn to the next exhibit, sir, Exhibit 24. That is also on 2nd May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pleso as well, the airport Pleso. You can see the crater of the explosion, and parts of the Orkan rocket, which fell several metres from the airport building. It did not fall within the premises of the airport building, but in the vicinity of the airport building.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, the rocket attack that took place on the next day, May 3rd, was that the rocket attack that took place and hit near the hospital and the old age home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 3rd May, yes, the centre of one of the explosions was right above the children's hospital in Klaiceva Street in Zagreb. In the immediate vicinity of the children's hospital, there is an old people's home, and in Dure Dezelica Street, there is the kindergarten. You can see the children's hospital in Klaiceva Street on the monitor. A pyrotechnician was killed here on this spot near the children's hospital while trying to defuse a bomblet. Mr Ivan Markulin, the late Ivan Markulin, father of two children.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 25 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these are the photographs of the shelling, the shelling of the city of Zagreb. On 3rd May 1995. A children's hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: The photographs depict that various windows et cetera were blown out of the children's hospital, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many glass windows were broken, smashed, at the children's hospital, and I remember that panic spread in the children's hospital at that moment. All children, and there were many of them in the hospital, were taken to the shelter of the basement, rooms which are by no means adequate as shelter. People were concerned, very nervous, about the children, about innocent children.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Just take a look at a sample. F8 depicts some of the damage within the hospital, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is on the ground floor. There is a gynaecological ward for ultrasound, for underaged persons. Unfortunately, you can see the results of the damage, glass splinters, furniture scattered around the room.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, you said that, in this location, a pyrotechnician working for the city of Zagreb was killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. He was killed there, Mr Markulin. We can see him on the photographs numbered 30. In spite of the fact that there was a hospital in the near vicinity, no one could help him. He had sustained very severe injuries and died.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn your attention to F31 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the late Ivan Markulin, photographed in the hospital in Klaiceva Street just several metres away from the spot where he was killed. I know this spot very well. This is the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Markulin was a pyrotechnician who was trained in defusing munitions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. On the first day, according to the information I have, he dismantled hundreds of such bomblets, and you see on the second day this thing happened to him while he was trying to dismantle one of those bomblets near the children's hospital. He was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, as you proceed through the photographs, we have another location in the area of the National Academy, beginning on F82.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Damage caused to the building of the Croatian National Theatre, photographs number 82 to 84. I remember that there were some actors rehearsing inside the theatre building at that moment, and several actors were injured as a result of the explosion of bomblets. I remember there were some foreign nationals among those actors. There was a Russian, an Englishman, a Rumanian actor, five or six of them.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Are there any military installations in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is the most beautiful part of the city of Zagreb, this is the building of the Croatian National Theatre which was built by the Austro-Hungarian Emperor. It is a beautiful building indeed, a very precious one.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Tuksa, you presented previously that in addition to the children's hospital being hit by the bomblets there was a home for the elderly that was also hit. Let me turn your attention to the next binder of photographs which is Exhibit 26. You can close that up and just go to 26.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the old people's home near the hospital in Klaiceva Street. Glass was broken here in the building of the old people's home. There were no injured civilians. We can only thank God for that.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: The last album we have of photographs is Exhibit 27 which is also on 3rd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the street called Ilica. A part of the rocket's mortar was found in Ilica Street. That is the most famous street of the city of Zagreb. You can see the crater caused by the rocket in front of the house number 68 in Ilica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: That will be photograph 11, the crater?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, photograph number 11.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: We will put that up on the monitor, your Honour. Again, this was a rocket that was dropped in the middle of a residential area where there were no military installations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I claim that there are no military installations in this part of the town of Zagreb, only residential buildings, hospitals, theatres, shops, and no city would have military installations at the centre of the town. You would usually have them in the suburb.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Tuksa, as part of the investigation, you were asked by Sergeant Curtis and others to put together a photo album of the various areas within the city of Zagreb that were hit with the bomblets, and how they looked on a normal day. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For six days rockets fell each day on the town of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question. Take a look at Exhibit 33.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can see the city of Zagreb here photographed 20 days after the incident. Just to show that it is really the centre of the town, the streets are very busy, and there are no -- these are the locations where bomblets fell on the city of Zagreb, the bomblets that were disbursed from the rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have not gone through every photograph that we have concerning the city of Zagreb and the various areas where the bomblets fell. We have produced them in photographs in Prosecution Exhibits 13 through 29, which we will make part of the record for your Honours' review. Prosecution Exhibit 33 is an exhibit that was put together by individuals working for Mr Tuksa, which shows the court what the city of Zagreb, the downtown portion of Zagreb that was attacked on 2nd and 3rd looks like on a normal day, looks like with normal civilian traffic to highlight the point of exactly what the intent was by Milan Marti and the RSK when this attack took place on 2nd and 3rd. That is the purpose of Prosecution Exhibit 33. We would ask that all these exhibits that have been reviewed, and I have just mentioned, be made part of the record for the purposes of this hearing. Your Honour, I have no further questions of Mr Tuksa. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr Tuksa, you confirmed that there was no military establishment in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there Headquarters or Ministry of War, or anything which could lead them to mistake it for military installations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we cannot speak about an attack on the Ministry of Defence, which is to the right hand of this location of explosions, eastward, because we can see that there was the National Theatre that was hit, and the Ministry of Defence is several kilometres to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Tuksa. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Tuksa, could I ask you whether or not during the course of these tragic events any other bombardments of Zagreb took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were only these two occasions when Zagreb was shelled. I am also aware of shelling in the area of Sisak and Karlovac, but I was not in charge of that investigation. The centre of Zagreb was never shelled, had never been shelled prior to that, as far as I know, not even during the Second World War. Nobody ever shelled Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have the feeling that, as regards the days following the shelling of Zagreb, that the victims, or in any case the civilian population, had the impression that they had been shelled in an abnormal way, in a particularly murderous manner? Here we are talking about terror and trying to terrorise the population. Did the press or the media print anything or say anything about any of the murderous and terrifying methods which had been used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a psychosis which reigned in Zagreb at the time. Civilians were aware of that, that they were being shelled in a very cunning way, a mischievous way. The media announced the news; there were no secrets. Everybody knew about it, and it was quite clear that the consequences were much less fatal the second day, because citizens, civilians, did not leave their homes on the second day. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you very much, Mr Tuksa. I do not think the Tribunal has any further questions for the witness. So that brings us to the end of the questions, and now, Mr Registrar, to protect the witness I would like to ask the curtains to be pulled down. The Tribunal, Mr Tuksa, would like to thank you for your testimony and for all the information you have given to the Judges regarding the events of the 3rd May. Thank you very much. Mr Prosecutor, before continuing, I would like to ask you where we stand as regards our work and also regarding the organisation aspects of today's work. During the conversation that we had, it was my feeling that we might be able to finish this evening. However, I would like to know how far we have got, where we stand, and also I would like to be sure that we can be assisted by interpreters who will be able to work until an hour which is not too late, even though it may well go beyond our planned time-schedule. We only want to do this if we can finish this evening, which will mean that we would not have to come back on Friday. So the floor is yours, Mr Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two brief witnesses, Mr Petric is a pyrotechnician who will answer the question of your Honour concerning how these bomblets were retrieved and why more were not detonated, and one final expert will be questioned by my colleague, Mr Ostberg. This is an expert, Major Ted Itani, who will give an overall expert opinion on the operation of the Orkan rocket when manned with these bomblets. That is i. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): I would consider that, given that the testimony is relatively brief, before we take a break, with the agreement of my colleagues, maybe we could listen to the shortest testimony, which would be Mr Mario Petric. Would this witness also like to benefit from the same protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Fine. Well, the curtains are down, so let us show into the Chamber Mr Mario Petric. Mr Mario Petric, good day. Before you take the oath, I would like to know whether you can hear what I am saying, in your own language, of course. Just a moment, Mr Mario Petric, I would like to know whether everything is going okay, whether you can hear the interpretation and whether you can hear me in your own language? If everything is okay, then I would like to invite you to read out the statement before you make your testimony. MARIO PETRIC, sworn

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you very much, Mr Petric. Please be seated. I would like to give the floor again to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr Petric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Original in Croatian) Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Petric, what do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Chief of the Anti-explosives Department of the Zagreb Police Department.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: How long have you been doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been working in the anti-explosive section for eight years, and I have been working in the police for 18 years.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: How long have you been the head of the Anti-explosives Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two years.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Petric, let me take you back to 2nd and 3rd May 1995. Do you recall those two days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you and men that were working for you called out to respond to a crisis in the city of Zagreb that took place on 2nd and 3rd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Explain to the court what happened and what your men did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2nd May, the city of Zagreb was shelled with cluster bomblets, which were fired from the Orkan rocket system. After the shelling, we were informed of the exact locations where the explosives occurred, where the shelling occurred in the city of Zagreb. We established an investigation team, and after the ambulance visited the scenes of the explosion we began with disposing of the explosive bomblets, together with the police who had been securing the sites, because there were lots of unexploded bomblets left from the explosion. All the bomblets are labelled KB1.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What exactly did you do to try to defuse these bomblets or to explode them at the scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we would locate a bomblet, if the technicians of the officers thought that they could deactivate it without any risk, they would do so by securing the fuse and unscrewing two screws which are fitted on the bomblet, and in that way they would deactivate the fuse, separate it from the body of the bomblet. They would be transported to a secure place, and would be activated later on.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Is this a dangerous procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a very dangerous procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Were any of your men, or people working for you, injured during the course of defusing these bomblets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one of my officers, Ivica Buksec was injured. His left arm had to be amputated and he sustained many shrapnel injuries all over his body. So he sustained severe bodily injuries. One of my officers, Ivan Markulin, was killed in the explosion of one of the bomblets.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Petric, let me turn your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 30. Do you have 30? Do you recognise those photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What were those photographs as a group, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph here shows, depicts, the motor, one part of the rocket which carries the cluster bomblets. On top of it there is a fuse marked with number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have a pen that you could point with to the various -- I guess you cannot do it here. It is okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: It is okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will use this pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: That is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph, here, depicts the motor of the rocket. This part here is the so-called container or cylinder where cluster bomblets are housed.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Do we see in that photograph, at 4, the size of the bomblets as they relate to the size of the rest of the rocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that under number 4. You can see a bomblet here, KB1.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: These photographs depict parts of the Orkan rockets that were retrieved after the attack on 2nd and 3rd May 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph shows the motor of the rocket, which belongs to the Orkan rocket system.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: And the next photograph, photograph 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also a rocket motor.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Photograph 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one as well, rocket motor.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Photograph number 5, rocket motor as well.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Photograph number 6, one part of the rocket motor. Number 7, photograph number 7, the cover of the cylinder or the container where the bomblets are housed. Photograph number 8 is also the cover of the cylinder or the container of the rocket. Photograph number 9 depicts the cover on which you can see the calibre of the rocket, and the label, the sign, the type of the rocket system, M-87. Photograph number 10 also depicts one part of the cover of the container of the rocket. Photograph number 11 shows the fuse which is situated on top of the rocket. It is called ITNA85B, which means instantaneous electronic fuse, and 85B. Photograph number 12 depicts cluster bomblets which are housed inside the cylinder or the container, the warhead of the rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Those are exactly the same as the one that is before you on the desk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Photograph number 13 shows a cluster bomblet. You can see separately the fuse and the body of the bomblet. Photograph number 16 shows the fuse and the tape, ribbon, which has two purposes: to arm the fuse and to stabilise the flight of the bomblet.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us stay with that photograph for one second, Mr Petric. How many unexploded bomblets did your unit retrieve or disarm on 2nd and 3rd May 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2nd May 1995, they collected approximately 500 of such bomblets.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: And how many on 3rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 3rd May it was less, because we had had one fatality and one severely injured officer in the meantime. So we continued with the disposal very slowly, and it took us a while.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say "a while", how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, around fifteen days. We spent fifteen days working, and then we decided -- we made sure that the great part of the work had been finished, and then we could fully guarantee that all of the bomblets had been retrieved.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: How many bomblets did you, in fact, retrieve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We retrieved around 1,599 bomblets. We defused 571 bomblets on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Is there any reason, to your knowledge, why these bomblets did not go off when they hit the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that there are several reasons. One of them is that the bomblets did not hit directly the object, the solid surface, but hit it at an angle and therefore could not be activated. Another reason I believe to be the fact that a small number of bomblets that were found, their fuses are not been armed. So an explosion could not have taken place because then the fire chain had not been established from the detonator cap to the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it, in fact, true, however, that many of these bomblets would have been exploded, as it turned out with one of your workers, merely through a little bit of a vibration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Very small movements of the plunger of the fuse may activate the detonator cap.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can complete the rest of the photographs, Sergeant Curtis, we should not have many left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Photograph number 17 shows the base, the part which is in contact with the cluster bomb, with the body of the cluster bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr Petric, based on your work in the area of pyrotechnics, and also examining these parts, do you know who made this product, who made this Orkan rocket with these cluster bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These bomblets bear the name of the manufacturer, or rather the abbreviation, Slavco Rodic, Bugojno. We suppose that the launching pads were built in Travnik, the launches were made in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Where is the manufacturer from these Orkan rockets from the initials that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is exactly correct, those factories where the property of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: That is known as the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: At the time this attack took place, did the Croatian armed forces have this rocket system, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Croatian army did not have this particular rocket system.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So, in conclusion, Mr Petric, over the course of time when individuals working for you were attempting to defuse these bomblets, one individual was permanently injured and one individual was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one individual was killed and another was seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of Mr Petric. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you, Mr Prosecutor. For clarification, you said that for some of the bombs they did not explode because the detonator was not charged. Was that by accident or was it done on purpose at the outset?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot answer your question very precisely. I do not know whether there was an intention to -- the cluster bomb, the warhead, has a time fuse setting. So this time can be programmed, computed, ahead of time, before the projectile hits the ground. If the rocket opens up relatively late, there is not enough time for all the bomblets to be armed, for all the fuses to be armed. Then, secondly, as a consequence of the flight, as a result of the flight of the bomblet, certain parts can simply fail to function. The fuse can fail to function. That may have been the reason why some bomblets did not explode. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you, Mr Petric. We would like to thank you for your evidence and all the technical precision you provided us with. We wish you a safe journey home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRIC
utterances.text: Good-bye, thank you. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Prosecutor, I suggest we adjourn now until 4.25. The session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRIC
utterances.text: JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Prosecutor, let me say before we introduce the next witness that we would like to hear some details about the level of protection for the witness. If it is the same level of protection as for the first one, then the Registrar will have to do somethin about the screens and the curtains, but please tell us more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: There will be no special protection for this witness. The witness I am calling is Major Ted Itani, as an expert witness on weapons. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Itani, firstly I would like to ask you whether you can hear me clearly in your own language, Mr Itani. Good, if you can hear me, and thank you very much. The Tribunal would like to thank you for coming along. Please read out the solemn oath. MAJOR TED ITANI, sworn

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you very much. Please be seated. Mr Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Major Itani. I use your military title, and I want you to start with telling the court something about your present occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am occupied in a variety of activities, starting with the most recent period after my retirement from the forces after some 40 odd years. I became a policy analyst, policy with respect to international relations, security and humanitarian issues, and at the same time, on an as required basis, I have also been a consultant on things such as anti-personnel mines and various weapon systems used by the armies of the world. That is based on my active military career in which there was a period in which I was an instructor, and perhaps at this stage I should add that my period in uniform started in 1953, and, in 1956, I went to the reserve army and the following year I became a Second Lieutenant officer in the reserve army. Two years later, I transferred to the regular force and was assigned to the artillery as an officer, and so my background is principally artillery. I did the usual tours of duty in various regiments in Canada and overseas, and, in 1974, I became an instructor and there followed about six years of instructional duties. In 1976/1977, for example, I was the senior instructor in gunnery at the combat training centre in Canada, in particular at the artillery school, where it was my pleasant duty to run a year long course. It was a technical and a tactical course designed to produce artillery instructors and artillery staff officers at the divisional level. That is a level of command which encompasses some 15,000 to 20,000 soldiers. Part of the training included the study of weapons design and munitions design, the employment, their tactical and technical limitations. I did that for two years, having successfully run two courses. That was followed by a year and a half to two years at the Combined Arms Operation School, where I taught tactics in combined arms operations. That is the integration of inventory and artillery units, armour, communications, engineers and logistics. Throughout all this, because of my background in artillery, it was my duty to teach fire support coordination, that is the coordination of direct fire weapons, which would be inventory, armour, indirect, which would be artillery, air support, and when necessary naval gun fire support. After a tour of duty in NATO Europe nearing the end of my career, my last 13 months of active duty was in the Balkans with the United Nations protection force. I spent 13 months there from October of 1992 to November of 1993. The first nine months was principally in Sarajevo where I was responsible for setting up the operational headquarters of the newly formed Bosnia-Herzegovina command, commanded by General Philipe Morillon. Later, I was assigned to establish a civil military co-operation function in the headquarters, and, finally, I was assigned as the Chief Determine to General Morillon. I suspect that it was because of General Morillon that I was eventually transferred to Zagreb where I joined the cabinet of General Jean Cotte, who was the force commander at that time. Throughout my Balkan tour of duty, one of the things that I opted to do with Commander Blessing was to teach crater analysis. It is a fairly simple process that was taught to artillery officers in the past, and it is a process that is designed to determine where the firing is coming from and the type of weapon. And, of course, I suggested that we follow this, because then it would extract a measure of accountability from the warring parties, particularly where humanitarian convoys and new troops were targeted with hostile military and mortar fire. Most recently I have been a policy consultant in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Canada, the Ministry of Defence, and last summer I was engaged by the Tribunal as a weapons specialist by one of the teams conducting their investigation into the siege of Sarajevo, mostly I was called by the Tribunal to join a team to go into Zagreb and then to come here to testify. That, sir, is my background.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. I feel confident that we have found ourselves an experienced expert witness. May I now start to ask you, are you familiar with the weapon called the Orkan system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am. It is a weapons system which was developed by the former Yugoslav national army. Most weapons systems take about fifteen years from the time of concept until the time that the actual production model is in the hands of the users. In this particular case, the research and development started in the mid-1980s, and the first line service type of system was in service by about 1992/1993. This is probably because it was a joint venture. In other words, the Yugoslav national army, in part, was funded by Iraq to conduct the research and development which accelerated the process. Therefore, this system is in service with the Iraqi army. A small number are in service with what was formerly called the Yugoslav national army. It came into service in the outbreak of the civil war. Because it came into service so recently in the development cycle there are some problems with it, and, undoubtedly, as the users gain experience, there will be product improvement to the system, to the munitions it carries, and perhaps it will expand to carry a variety of other munitions. Who is to say? Only the imagination of humanity can limit what type of weapons we can create to destroy one another.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: You said something about this weapon being produced and used in the Yugoslav army. Do they have this on their inventory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They do now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: They do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you tell the court something about the amount of this kind of system in the hands of the Serbian Krajina army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would certainly be in the hands of the Bosnian Serb Army and the former RSK Army. Perhaps you will recall that the line of support that came to the Bosnian Serb Army also served the RSK Army through the Posedena corridor in north-eastern Bosnia. The numbers are not large. Therefore, they attempt to be a very valuable delivery system. Therefore, I would suspect they are granted a great deal of protection and concealment.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: You say that the amount is not great. What would you suggest that it would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps a dozen delivery systems at the most. There are likely to be more coming into service.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you, then, proceed to tell us something about this delivery system, maybe show the court how this system operates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may have --

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: I think you may start with exhibit number 34, which will also be in the hands of the court, I think, please, Major Itani.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The lower picture in this exhibit shows the M-87 Orkan rocket launcher in its tactical mode. That is to say, the weapon is ready to fire. The upper picture shows, I would say, probably a manufacturer's picture, and what it shows -- the instrument that is sticking out from one of the tubes is a tube that is used in reloading it, and in calibrating the electronics and taking measurements. I will say more about that later. The system can fire twelve rockets, with a maximum range of 50 kilometres. A rocket can carry a variety of warheads. It can carry what is known as dual purpose improved conventional munitions. That is a fairly large description to describe something as simple as a bomblet. That, in weapons parlance, is what we call a dual purpose improved conventional munitions, because it is designed for anti-personnel use as well as anti-armour, because the shaped charge in this particular bomblet can penetrate up to 60 millimetres of armour, and perhaps I can explain a bit more about that later. The rocket has a solid propellant fuel. 10 kilograms is the booster fuel and the 130 kilograms is a sustaining motor.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you now, please, move maybe to Exhibit 35, which shows the rocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first exhibit, from left to right, approximately the left half of that rocket would comprise the rocket motor. That is the propellant. 10 kilograms is designed to expel the rocket from its launcher tube. This takes 200 milliseconds and it provides 8,000 kilograms of thrust, of pushing power. Immediately, the sustaining motor ignites and it burns for approximately five seconds, producing some 18,000 kilograms of thrust. So the effect at the launcher end is that, if you were to witness such an event, the first impression you would get is a loud bang or an explosion. That is the booster rocket firing to clear the launcher rocket tube. That would be followed instantaneously by a loud roar, a smaller explosion and a loud roar that sustains for approximately five seconds providing that rocket with 18,000 kilograms of thrust. Needless to say, this creates a great disturbance at the launcher end of smoke and debris. Therefore, a launch is very easily detected. If the launch is easily detected, it also means that that launcher is liable for retaliatory action. Therefore, a detachment can put the launcher into action and fire it in under five minutes. This precludes a travel time that it takes from somewhere where it is hidden under cover in the woods or in a warehouse or some other place. It will be deployed on to a launch pad, fired and then redeployed and withdrawn very quickly to another location where it will be reloaded.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is where it is on wheels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It has four axels which provide the power, four axels in the truck. If we can move on to the next exhibit, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see that the construction is relatively sophisticated. It shows the motor end of it, and you note the perforations at the end of it. This is to ensure that the thrust that is provided both by the booster and the sustaining motor is even, so that there will be no wobble in the rocket. As well as the fins that deploy after the rocket clears, the launcher tube provides stability.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you like to go to number 36?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: 37, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 37 is the warhead portion, and here there is a variation in the number of bomblets that the warhead holds. The number varies between anywhere from 260, 285 to 288. I opt for 288, because I suspect that it is a result of product improvement. Similarly, the number of stainless steel pellets wrapped around the body of this bomblet varies from 400 to 420 to 450. I opt for 450, because it is probably a result of product improvement.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you like to go to exhibit 38?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is just a single rocket. It leaves this launch pad on the left-hand side of the paper, of this diagram, and its maximum height at maximum range is shown diagrammatically at a pre-set height. The warhead is timed to open by a small explosive charge releasing these bomblets. The optimum height of burst is 400 metres, but obviously there will be some errors. All systems will have delivery errors where they will release too low or too high. In any case, with the standard delivery height of 400 metres, one can expect a single rocket to disburse rockets over an area of approximately 150 metres wide and 200 metres long. That pattern would be elliptical. That is one rocket. Picture, if you will, six rockets being aimed at the same target, or three rockets, and there you can picture a large area being saturated by these bomblets, an area that could be 500 metres by 500 metres, or as large as 1,200 metres by 1,200 metres. The system, with its various munitions, is designed for very specific use. In the case of most systems employing the dual purpose improved conventional munitions, it is designed for use against soft military targets. That is to say, targets that have little or no protection, such as troops in the open; such as installations and supply depots where there are fuel dumps or ammunition dumps; communications centres that have not been hardened, that is to say communications that have not been put underground into bunkers. It can also be used against mass formations of armour, that is to say armoured personnel carriers and tanks that are deployed in an area of, say, 1,000 metres by 1,000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you say something in this context about the accuracy of the rocket in context with the target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The system is designed as an area weapon, therefore one cannot expect pinpoint accuracy. At maximum range, you can expect an area of as much as 600 metres, plus or minus of the intended target, and to the left and right of it. So that is a large circle of probability of air. It can be almost indiscriminate, in fact, the probable area is so high, but undoubtedly there will be product improvements as the system gets used more frequently, and changes are made to the system. The distinction here, I think, that is important, is that it is a rocket and therefore it has no guidance system, as opposed to a missile system that can be terminally guided on to a target. By terminal, I mean that, in the last parts of its trajectory, the weapon can be accurately directed on to a specific building, perhaps, or a specific tank or armoured personnel carrier or a bunker. This system does not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: We have heard many times today the term "missile" being used instead of "rocket". This is a rocket.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a rocket, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: The distinction between these two is that the rocket will fire it and aim at something and then you leave it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: And the missile you can guide to its target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally in the weapons world that is how we define the difference between a missile and a rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. In this context, six were fired one day, and six were fired the other day. I think you would like to show us maybe some pictures and comment on the impact of these rockets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I may move on to Exhibit 22.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Particularly photographs F5 and F6. This is a school yard which I visited last week, and here it shows that the weapon was not appropriate to the target. The bomblets, which impacted along the side of the school, did very little damage.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: How come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it was not designed to take on such hardened installations. Secondly, the bomblets are not sufficiently strong to take out or destroy buildings. There are other weapons systems that are more suited to that task: particularly in terms of destructive force and in terms of accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you take the opportunity, when you have this bomblet in your hand, to explain to the court how it functions when it explodes and what exactly happens and how it happens, really?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The 288 bomblets that are housed in the warhead portion of the rocket are placed in there much like a honeycomb, and at a given moment, at a pre-set time, the outer skin, or the membrane of the warhead explodes and these bomblets are released. At the time of release, they are all safe bomblets. This tape has two purposes. First, it is to provide stability to reduce the dampening effect of oscillation. In the case of photographs F4 and F5, you will see that it was not particularly successful in dampening that oscillation, because it hit the side of the building probably this way. What it is designed to do is land on the target like that, so that it can function in two modes, anti-personnel and anti-armour, that is to say bore a hole through the hull of a tank or an armoured personnel carrier, by what is called a shaped charge inside. The second function of the ribbon is that as it floats down from the release height, it turns and twists and in the process it unscrews. Can you see that, where it unscrews? Now the firing pin is free and it is floating. Up to that time, although the firing pin was there, it was fixed and immovable, which rendered this bomblet safe. At the same time that the screw is unscrewed to its full length, there is a sliding detent which comes out. What that does is clear a fire tube from the initiator to the charge inside, so that any jarring of it will cause the initiator to explode the filling inside. If that detent were inside, then of course that would not happen. So a bomb disposal expert, or a pyrotechnician will look at it and he would be very careful if that detent were exposed like that. If it were to be inside and held firm, then it is a relatively safe bomblet to render safe by removing the initiating portion of the bomblet.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then would you take the opportunity, also, to say something about the steel balls, the 450 steel balls.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The 450 steel balls, upon impact, when the bomblet explodes, will disburse in a pattern of 360 degrees in all directions, at about three times the speed of sound. Its lethal radius is ten metres. It can cause --

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of one steel ball?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. If it were to strike your eye, for instance, it could penetrate your brain, into your brain. Or some other vital organ can be hit by a steel ball. The radius around which casualties can be produced can be as far as 50 metres. Compounding that, of course, are the parts of this bomblet that will also fan out, radiate out, in 360 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you, then, maybe proceed to comment on some of these photographs which we have shown you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If I may return to F5 and F6 of Exhibit 22, what I found significant was the very limited damage to the building. Fortuitously no personnel injuries, because the children were not out in the yard. The third thing I noticed, as I walked around, was that there was no evidence of this school ever being a military installation.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Please go on, take the next photo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 13, photograph F4. What was significant to me about this photograph, and also having visited there, was that I could not conceive of a military installation being at this locality. F33 is typical of what happens to soft targets such as street cars, passenger cars, light military trucks, the anti-personnel and the anti-armour capabilities of this bomblet shattering windows and injuring people. F40, the injuries are consistent with her being at least within ten metres of a bomb exploding. It appears to me she might have been actually struck by a bomblet. F58. Even with the protection of being in a car, the effects can be fatal. Later examination of other photographs for this victim revealed that the major injuries were to the right-hand side of this person's head, which indicates to me that the bomblet probably hit the centre of the car, just where the windscreen joins the top of the car, that is where it exploded, and as a result much of the explosive force was sustained by the victim. F89 and F90. Here you see the results of the dual effects, that is the anti-armour effect of this bomblet, and the anti-personnel effects. The small holes that are radiating out from the big gaping hole are made by these standard steel balls. The big hole itself is made by the shaped charge that is contained within this bomblet.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could anyone survive sitting in this car being hit by the bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very doubtful. Very doubtful. If one of the shaped charges does not do its damage, then the steel pellets will. Even being inside a building does not guarantee protection, as shown in F97 and F98. Here, obviously, some of the pellets and parts of the bomb went through the door and through the window, and perhaps the door was open at the time, resulting in another victim.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: This person was inside the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the building. So the burst could have occurred from one of these bomblets hitting something higher along the building, or hitting the top of a cab or a car or a truck, or even landing on the ground, as intended, in its proper attitude and exploding that way, killing the person here.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do you have any more you want to comment on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be about it. I think the rest are much the same, in other words supportive of what I have been saying, the effects of this weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: We thank you. I have some further questions. The witness examined prior to you today told us that the substantial amount of the bomblets never did explode. Will you please comment on that and give an explanation as to what happens to the bomblets that do not explode?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There could be a number of reasons why it did not explode. For one thing, if the height, the 400 metre height of burst was not achieved for a particular reason, perhaps it was too low, then the bomblet would not have had the time to spin sufficiently to free the floating firing pin. That could be one cause. The second cause is that, with a low burst of altitude, the oscillation was not dampened and so the bomblet could have struck the side of a building and landed on its side rather than on its base. The large numbers of unarmed, so to speak, bomblets that could be recovered still pose a danger, as would be the case with those that are armed, and it is a residual danger that can last for many, many years, because if it is soft ground these things can get buried 25, 30 centimetres, and at some future date, through frost action or farming activity or construction, these could be dug up and accidentally exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: So they will not be rendered useless if they do not explode when they hit the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: There are a few other things I would like to know. Could you tell us something about from what area, from what place, these rockets were launched at Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time that it happened, and with my memory of the confrontation lines as they were at that time, it was launched from an area called Sector North under the old United Nations protection force, the four sectors that were established by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: We might put it under the ELMO and see if you can give us some guidance. You have it before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Zagreb being in the top left-hand corner of this photograph, if you can go to the south-west, approximately 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, please point with your pen, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is about the area. That is a line, approximately Carlon Vacglina Vergonmost. That particular area was under the control of the RSK at the time that the Orkan rockets were launched. Since coming back into Theater, I have driven into that area and the area is suitable, because it is laced with good, hard roads. Many possibilities for hiding these launchers, and many possibilities to reload these launchers under concealment: it makes good tactical sense to launch from an area that offers all those.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Which is the distance from there to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just under 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: So it is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is well within range.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: I think you have given us all we need to know about this rocket. A final question again, this rock you said can be used for many different reasons. It can be fitted to hit military targets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: If the aim was, in this particular case, to hit a military target, how would it then have been fitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: If somebody tells us that the shelling of Zagreb was a military operation, and that the aim of the operation was to hit military targets, was it suitably fitted to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not have used an Orkan system to attack a military target in Zagreb. It is a built up area. I would have used some other system that would have provided me with appropriate precision, and appropriate destructive force. As I indicated, a shaped charge does only localised damage. The other purpose, the anti-personnel feature of this weapon, does localised damage. So it is not a weapon of great destruction. The destructive capability, although tragic, as you have seen, is very limited, particularly because of its shaped charge. For instance, ordinary bomblets, perhaps, might have been more effective in this particular instance. But my preference would have been to use precision guided munitions of heavy calibre, such as a 250 pound bomb with a laser-guided nose, so that you could take out specific installations.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do you consider this type of weapon, with these bomblets, to have some kind of a terror effect on the population of a city hit by it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Being an artillery officer, I am, of course, aware of the use of artillery for purposes other than military. And as well having spent nine months in Sarajevo I entered Sarajevo at a fairly noisy time in Sarajevo's life in October of 1992, and there is no doubt that a population that lives under terror of bombardment, regardless of the meaning, is a population that is easily manipulated, and it is something that I saw firsthand during my tour in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. I have concluded my questions. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you, Mr Prosecutor. My colleagues, would you like to ask any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr Itani, could you briefly conclude that the use of the Orkan rockets is, as an expert, a means to cause indiscriminate damage and cannot reach very specific targets owing to the fact, as you said, that the range of error is, I quote you, 600 square metres, so it cannot fairly be used to reach very precise targets. Could we conclude that from your very enlightening description?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I would like to emphasise that, when I said 600 metres, that is at maximum range of the rocket, where it can go 600 metres plus of the target. It can go 600 metres minus of the target, or 600 metres to the left of it or to the right of it. Therefore, if the target is a purely military one that is disbursed over a wide geographic area, then really the inaccuracy of the system is irrelevant. You can conclude that it is a rather indiscriminate delivery system from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Mr Itani, I have two questions for you. As far as you know, has this particular weapon been used elsewhere, whether elsewhere in the world, during other conflicts, or elsewhere in the conflict concerning the former Yugoslavia, or was this the first time that this arm has been used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this weapons system was used during the Gulf War by the Iraqi forces, not with great effect, because the weapons system was not sufficiently developed to bring about the desired results, but it was used nevertheless. In the Balkan wars, I am not aware of a specific instance in which this system was used using this type of ammunition, but I am aware that the system is available in that in my time in Sarajevo many of our UN observers reported sightings of this delivery system. As well, many of our own UN observers who have served in Croatia have reported the sighting of this system. So we know that it is in the inventory of the army of the Bosnian Serbs and the army of the RSK. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Regarding the destructive effects, the damaging effects caused by this weapon, as a specialist in this area, could you compare these effects with other prohibited arms within international law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would not fit into the category of a prohibited conventional weapon. Its effect has been in existence for many, many years. It is a fairly simple principle, the use of the shaped charge, to defeat light armour, and this principle has been in use since before the Second World War. The fact that it has been miniaturised to this extent, of course, has been a natural development. Some of you may recall in the Second World War a shaped charge which was used against tanks. It was much larger than this, and much more cumbersome, and yet today a weapon that small, a bomblet that small, can penetrate, through a shaped charge, an armoured personnel carrier, or a tank in areas where it does not have sufficient armour or armour that is thinner than 60 millimetres. It is not a prohibited weapon, at least not yet. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you very much. I do not have any other questions. On behalf of my colleagues I would also like to say, personally, to you that we are grateful to you, Mr Itani, for your testimony. We would like you to go back to your work, so the Tribunal thanks you. Mr Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We have offered the evidence we would like to bring to this Rule 61 hearing and offered you the exhibits and testimonies. What is left to be done, looking, in front of me, on the Rule 61 procedures in case of failure to execute a warrant of arrest, is that the Trial Chamber shall have the relevant parts of the indictment read out by the Prosecutor, together with an account of the efforts to effect the service referred to in sub-rule (a) above. I think, your Honours, in my opening statement I gave a summary of the indictment and the counts which we charge Milan Martic. I do not think there is any need for me to read the counts again. Do your Honours feel comfortable with the way I have done it already? Then what I have to do, I think, is to give an account of the efforts to effect service referred to in sub-rule (a). That I will do now, if it pleases the court. I go back to the document which I submitted to your Honour Judge Jorda on 12th February 1996 in which I listed the different things we did to try to effect this service. I do a summary now, and I go to tell you exactly what has been done. On 25th July 1995, an indictment against Milan Martic was confirmed by Judge Jorda and warrants for arrest were issued, being directed to the Republic of Croatia, to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Warrants and orders which were to be sent to the self-proclaimed Republic of Krajina in Knin could not be submitted because this entity ceased to exist a few days after the indictment was confirmed, that is in the beginning of August last year. Upon an application of the Prosecutor, the Trial Chamber presided over by Judge Karibi-Whyte requested, on 2nd August 1995, each member state of the United Nations to transmit to the Prosecutor any information it may possess concerning the location of Milan Martic, including his travels, and this request was transmitted on August 3rd and August 4th 1995, to the ministries of every member state at the United Nations in New York. Following a request by the Prosecutor, the Registrar on 23rd January 1996 requested the diplomatic representatives of the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the Netherlands to arrange for the publication of the indictment upon Milan Martic in newspapers having wide circulation in these states, and to finish it, what we have heard already today, as evidence, Milan Martic acknowledged to television, to radio, to journalists, his awareness of the indictment in discussing it. The last time, just three days ago, 24th February, he said that he was aware of it and that he would come, but he gave some reasons why he would not. That, I think, is what I have to report on what is done to serve this indictment on the accused. Thank you. The last thing I do before we are ready to conclude from the Prosecution is to mention Section E of Rule 61, saying that if the Prosecutor has satisfied the Trial Chamber that the failure to effect personal service was due in whole or in part to a failure, or refusal of a state to co-operate with the Tribunal in accordance with Article 29. We do not. We cannot point at any special statement they did not co-operate with. Of course, we do not know what different states have done or have not done. That is what I have to say. What we could do, with some final statements from my colleague, Mr Kehoe. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Excuse me, Mr Prosecutor, could I just go back over something? Sorry. Could I just go back to paragraph E? If we read in the same paragraph, paragraph E, just to refer back to that again, could I point your attention to the following? It is at your initiative to establish whether the failure to effect personal service was due in whole or in part to a failure or refusal of a state to co-operate. So, quite clearly, it is not for the Tribunal to take the initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): However, would you kindly develop for us your point of view here, in my opinion at the very least it would be desirable to have an explanation of this particular context. You are, after all, saying simultaneously that you have undertaken all possible measures regarding the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Knin authorities, and I suppose also regarding the Croatian authorities, and then also you go on to say that you are not requesting of the Tribunal that it should say that one state in particular should be imputed responsible for this fault, this failure to effect personal service. Are these two attitudes, these two approaches consistent? I have not fully understood that. Could you give us more details about it? It is an important point. Let me remind you that it is on the basis of this particular article that the President of the Tribunal, at the order of the Chamber, indicated the failure to act on the part of a particular state to the Securities Council. Therefore, it is one of the foundation stones, one of the major resources at the disposal of the Tribunal, because we need the co-operation. In fact, the co-operation of member states is obligatory. They must co-operate with the Tribunal. So, Mr Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could, with a good foundation, say this state did not do what we wanted them to do, but the questions that we have are questions like "we would, if we could". But I would not stand in this court and say state X did not do this and this is on the ground of a failure or a refusal to co-operate with the Tribunal. I have no foundation, no grounds, to bring an accusation of that kind against any special state. Therefore, I abstain from invoking paragraph E in the submissions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr Prosecutor, if you have reached the state where the indicted person is residing where you think he is, you do not need to prove any commission of an act. It is omission, and the proof of an omission carries itself evidently. How can you prove an omission?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is certainly not easy. In this Article from 24th April, indeed we know where this person were to be found. Now there are grounds to believe that he may be in Banja Luka, I do not know. But in the Office of the Prosecutor, we have found no way to ask the Tribunal or the President, go to the Securities Council to bring this notice in Article E. So I simply do not make any submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you, Mr Prosecutor. There are no other questions. I think our work on Rule 61 on Martic is closed. The Tribunal will deliberate in order to find out whether we can confirm, or reconfirm the indictment. For this purpose, we will adjourn and we will give our opinion on Friday, 8th march. I am sorry, there was one additional point. I thought you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We had in mind to give some summing-up remarks. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Fine. I give the floor to your colleague. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In all due respect, your Honour, if you do not think it is necessary, the Prosecutor does not want to give the court anything the court does not want. Quite briefly, to go through our positions, your Honour, on -- JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Not at all. Even a judge can make or commit an error. I ask the Prosecutor to give me explanations, and also I ask my colleagues as regards this failure to appear. I understand that you would like to submit your final comments and we do not have to go into great details. You have the floor. Closing Statement by MR KEHOE

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We called upon your Honours in the Rule 61 hearing to give the Tribunal reasonable cause to believe that Milan Martic has committed the crime set forth in the indictment. The crimes set forth in the indictment are violations of the laws and customs of war. Your Honours have heard the facts that have been set forth here today. What happened, with Milan Martic as President of the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina, was a terrorist act. They mobilised through the words of General Celeketic to attack the civilian population if they got involved in any type of armed confrontation with the Republic of Croatia. Any type of armed confrontation with the Republic of Croatia was going to trigger an attack on the civilian population in one of the major cities in Croatia. They promised to do that, and when, in fact, Western Slavonia was attacked on the morning of May 1st, 1995, by the armies of the Republic of Croatia referred to on these occasions as "the HV", the response by the Republic of Serb Krajina was the terrorist attack, the missile attack on the civilian population of the city of Zagreb.
