What was the intent there? The intent quite clearly was not to go after military targets. There were no military targets in downtown Zagreb on May 2nd, on May 3rd, or at any other time. The intent of those attacks was to murder civilians and to terrorise the population. They were successful. Civilians were murdered on the streets. An individual was waiting for his wife who was out shopping. Another individual, a woman, happened to be in a tram, and about to get off at a popular square, possibly to do some shopping in the middle of the day. Individuals were murdered as they went about their course of business, doing what normal pedestrians do, at every major city, be it Paris, be it Rio de Janeiro, New York or any other place. The law as it is structured, your Honours, is designed to protect those people. The clear position of the Prosecutor on a customary law is that reprisals of any form, in any fashion, against a civilian population are illegal. That particular position was enunciated in UN Resolution 2675 in 1970 that was unanimously adopted by the UN Security Council and the UN General Assembly. That particular resolution unanimously adopted stated that all reprisals against civilians are forbidden. This Appellate Chamber, in discussing the jurisdictional aspects of the Tadic motion, referred to Resolution 2675 and adopted and commented that Resolution 2675 is now customary law, customary law that protects the civilian population of any place against reprisals, in any way, shape or form. Even if one looks at more conventional law, the law of war, as time has moved on and humanitarian law has moved with the law of war, the primary concern of the movement has been towards humanitarian concerns, not rigid, distinctions between states that are involved in internal conflicts and international conflicts, but the guiding light throughout all of this is moving down towards protecting civilians, protecting those people who are walking about their day-to-day affairs, going to the store, taking their children to work, going to school, et cetera. Even if one looks at conventional law, your Honours can conclude that reprisals against civilians are forbidden, be it an international or an internal conflict. Clearly, on Protocol I reprisals against the civilian population in international conflicts are forbidden per Article 51. It is specifically forbidden, so we need not even discuss it. Under Protocol II, which refers to internal conflicts, the guiding principle, the ideological approach of Protocol II is the safeguarding of civilians. While there is no specific delineation saying that reprisals against civilians are forbidden in Protocol II, there is (1) clearly an attitude among the signees of Protocol II to protect civilians and (2) clearly there was no intent, when Protocol II was being ratified and negotiated with individuals, to allow for reprisals against civilians. In fact, if one looks at the legislative history behind Protocol II, you examine that the failure to specifically preclude reprisals did not in any way, shape or form mean that reprisals against civilians in the internal context were allowed. There were several reasons, when you examine the legislative history for that particular provision to be excluded, some political, some legal. Some individuals were not happy with the actual language, but there was no one during those proceedings that came forward to say, "We are voting for or against, because we think that reprisals should be allowed against civilians in an internal context". It just is simply contrary to our now attitude of humanitarian law. If one looks at the commentary for Protocol II that is set forth by the ICRC, who one might say is one of the leading eyes on humanitarian law throughout the world, quite clearly in the commentaries of Protocol II, the ICRC says that reprisals against civilians in Protocol II are forbidden. Any way we look at it, your Honours, be it in the international context or internal conflict, it makes simply no difference. At this stage of humanitarian law, and where we are in customary law and conventional law, it is the position of the Prosecutor that reprisals and attacks on the civilian population in any way, shape or form are illegal. In this particular case, when we look at those facts and we look at the intent behind what Milan Martic ordered, he did what he promised to do some months prior. He promised that he was going to attack the civilian population; he did attack the civilian population, and he successfully carried out the murder and the dismemberment in some cases and certainly the wounding of civilians that were walking about on their daily way going from various locations. The Prosecutor submits that such conduct simply cannot be tolerated as humanitarian law moves into the 21st century. At this point, your Honours, we respectfully request that the Tribunal and the court confirm the indictment and that the Prosecution has successfully met its burden under Rule 21. Thank you. JUDGE JORDA (original in French): Thank you, Mr Prosecutor. Sorry that I stopped before your final summing-up. I would like to turn and ask my colleagues if they have any final questions or comments? No. I would like to say the meeting is now closed. The Tribunal will deliberate on this, and give its decision on Thursday, 8th March in the morning. The session is closed. I would also like to thank the booths and the interpreters who have always worked very efficiently and effectively.
